title: Kumai-218
dek: An ancient warforged who prepares fighters through difficult tests, calls for a wartime plan and expects results beyond the arena. His judgment can recognize courage and good thinking while his methods provoke real objections.

body:
Kumai-218 is present long before the company that becomes the Veilguard. The quest record describes an ancient warforged who keeps an old arena, trains fighters and presses people to turn intentions into decisions. His severity can expose weakness, but it also creates friction with those he expects to teach.

March 2024 · the old arena

He welcomes fighters brought by Melian. He says he has made a long-lost gladiatorial colosseum his home and that Melian agreed to establish a settlement nearby. This is his account of their earlier connection, rather than an independently dated founding chronology.

Kumai explains that the arena’s magic prevents deaths and requires participants to face both one another and his constructs. The aim is adaptation under pressure. He recognizes Quake’s tactical precision, and the scene ends with Quake taking the contest.

John’s refusal to fight his companions challenges that method. Kumai calls him noble while questioning whether such restraint can survive war. He warns of betrayal but cannot answer away John’s commitment to sacrifice for others. The exchange preserves a disagreement about what preparedness should cost.

June 2025 · asking for a plan

During the Rahu crisis he calls the community together and insists that temporary success does not replace a strategy. He asks what they can offer, which risks they will accept and how they will keep fighting when powerful adventurers must leave.

His advice remains advice: he does not claim to know everything and tells the participants that they must convince one another. He describes his own responsibility as protecting the arena. In a later June exchange he also promises help defending the town while others are away. Neither act makes him Pristinia’s sole commander.

April 2026 · hearts before competence

Kumai asks Lady Severina, Pelagia, Thorn, Camilla Blackwood, Kasiri Ruza and Modeli to define leadership, honor and wisdom. He follows with hypothetical dilemmas involving loyalty, truth, sacrifice and victory. These are examination scenarios, not events the candidates actually carried out.

He then asks whom they would follow into battle. Support for Severina establishes peer trust, but does not finish the test. He returns in new armor with a sword and joins a free-for-all arena fight as another participant.

His automatons remove and revive him after he falls. Kasiri defeats Thorn at the end of the contest; Kumai praises her and tells the group to discuss their leader and report back. The outcome distinguishes martial success from final appointment. The earlier Vanguard remains a separate history from the new company.

May 2026 · results beyond the arena

He returns to the question of whether the trainees have acted on their lessons. A field test sends them after awakened undead and their leader. The choice to use that danger draws objections; his insistence that it is useful training remains his judgment.

When the group returns with the head, Severina credits Moira with uncovering the puzzle. Kumai’s sharp manner gives way to a brief acknowledgment of work well done. His standards include understanding a problem, rather than merely surviving a fight.

The open history

The meaning of his number, the full history of the arena and the extent of his formal institutional authority remain unresolved. He is not established as the Vanguard’s founder or sole membership authority. His teaching has a consistent concern with preparedness, while the people he teaches retain the right to disagree with its methods.

The pupil who refuses the lesson

At the old arena, Kumai’s announced purpose is to prepare heroes. That does not make every visitor welcome as a trainee: when Quake asks about bringing the militia, he demands that they first prove worthy. He wants fighters who can adapt under pressure, and warns that his constructs hunt people who try to avoid the fight.

John’s refusal to attack his companions irritates him and then catches his interest. Kumai orders the constructs after John, watches blows repeatedly fail and jokes that even the machines seem to like him. Calling John noble does not stop him from arguing that a warrior must be ready for betrayal. John answers that he will sacrifice himself to give others time; Kumai cannot simply dismiss that commitment.

Meanwhile he notices tactical work, including Quake’s precision, and takes requests for refreshments. Constructs go to see about flowers when Scribonia asks. His attention moves between severe instructions, practical observation and the comfort of the people watching. The arena is his home as well as his test.

He calls a council, not a command to obey

During the Rahu crisis, Kumai brings the company to a table and asks how they intend to recover Melian and keep fighting. He rejects the idea that a recent victory solves the war. Paying with magical artifacts might buy an immediate answer while strengthening an enemy who could return. More powerful adventurers also have a wider war to fight and cannot stay indefinitely.

He asks the group to weigh proposed exchanges, ambushes, captures and negotiations. When he lacks information, he says so. When someone offers a tactic, he tells them to convince their companions: protecting the arena is his own responsibility. Calling the meeting does not make every choice his order.

By the end he accepts that they have a strategy, even while saying it is not the one he would have chosen. His severity has pushed a decision without producing agreement with him. The separate later promise to help defend the town remains a contribution, not proof that he became its sole commander.

A test that sends objections into the field

When the new company meets him again, Kumai dismisses its speeches, name and medallions as inadequate evidence of progress. He acknowledges Kasiri’s earlier victory, then sends the group toward awakened dead and demands their leader’s head. He says he, or Namo’o, has roused them; the scene establishes the claim he makes to the company rather than an independently witnessed act of awakening.

Kasiri objects to the use of undead, Camilla points to the attack they have just fought off and Modeli challenges the danger he is imposing. Kumai defends the exercise, treats survival as a measure of readiness and makes clear that the targets can take bodies. His justification does not make the trainees’ objections disappear. The task is outside the arena; its earlier assurances about preventing death cannot simply be assumed here.

He does notice good reasoning. Kasiri works out a danger from his warning, while Karnak’s attempt to display a weapon leaves him visibly astonished at the missed point. When the party returns with a head, his expectant smile changes into surprise. Severina credits Moira with solving the puzzle. Kumai’s response becomes brief and unadorned praise, and he lets Camilla keep the skull. The scene ends with an achieved task, not unanimous approval of the teacher’s methods.

profile.personality: Severe, observant and impatient with speeches. He can mock John’s restraint, appreciate it, call for refreshments and praise a solution in a few plain words. His judgments are forceful and remain open to disagreement.
profile.achievements: Keeps the old arena, tests early arrivals, calls a Rahu war council, participates in the later vanguard contest and sets a field task that the company completes. Neither the arena’s safeguards nor his own account of divine assistance is generalized beyond its source context.
profile.relationships: Melian brings early candidates, Quake earns his tactical respect and John challenges the cost of his training. Severina, Kasiri, Camilla, Thorn and their companions meet his later tests. The field task ends with Severina giving Moira credit, which Kumai acknowledges without his usual sharp reply.
